records.sourceFile: Effect of Sleep Duration and Concussion History on Neurocognitive Testing Symptoms for Post-injury States.pdf

paper.citation: Ezzat B, Hrabarchuk E, Lemonick M, Rentzeperis F, Kalagara R, Ali M, et al. Effect of Sleep Duration and Concussion History on Neurocognitive Testing Symptoms for Post-injury States. Clin J Sport Med. 2024;00:1-7.
paper.abstract: Retrospective observational study of 5,349 student-athletes aged 12 to 22 who had post-concussion ImPACT and PCSS assessments at urban concussion centers in Colorado and Florida (2009 to 2019). Multivariable linear regression related hours of sleep the night before testing to symptom scores, controlling for age, sex, ADHD, learning disability and number of prior concussions. Less sleep was associated with higher total symptom scores in athletes with and without a prior concussion, and the associations with specific symptoms were mixed.
paper.tldr: In this registry of adolescent athletes, fewer hours of sleep before post-concussion testing went with higher total symptom scores, whether or not the athlete had a prior concussion. Specific symptom associations were inconsistent, so sleep and concussion history should be weighed alongside symptoms rather than used alone.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis of ImPACT and PCSS registry data, restricted to post-injury assessments. Athletes were grouped by no prior concussion (n = 2,671) or one or more prior concussions (n = 2,678), and sleep was categorized as under 7, 7 to 9, or over 9 hours. Multivariable linear regression tested sleep hours against neurologic, psychiatric and total symptom scores and against individual PCSS symptoms, controlling for age, sex, ADHD, learning disability and prior concussion count.
paper.findings: Total symptom score was negatively associated with sleep hours in athletes without a prior concussion (b = -0.007, 95% CI -0.011 to -0.003; P = 0.0006) and with one (b = -0.009, 95% CI -0.012 to -0.005; P < 0.0001), while neurologic and psychiatric scores were not significantly associated. In Table 4, vomiting and difficulty concentrating were negatively associated with sleep in athletes without a prior concussion; in athletes with a prior concussion, headache, irritability and difficulty concentrating were negatively associated, but light sensitivity, numbness and feeling slowed down were positively associated (more symptoms with more sleep). Athletes without a prior concussion had higher total, neurologic and psychiatric symptom scores than those with one (total 21.5 vs 15.1; P < 0.0001).
paper.limitations: The design is retrospective, sleep is self-reported for the night before testing, and concussion severity was not measured, so causal and clinical inference is limited. The Results text describes headache in the prior-concussion group as worsening with longer sleep despite a negative coefficient, and the Abstract gives a different light-sensitivity estimate (b = 0.10) and a malformed confidence interval for difficulty concentrating; this record uses the Table 4 values. Effect sizes are small, sleep was entered as the dependent variable, and the authors note the mean sleep difference between groups (7.7 vs 7.6 hours) is not clinically significant.
paper.practicalImplications: When recording post-concussion symptoms, also record the night's sleep hours and the number of prior concussions, because both are associated with symptom scores in this study. Read symptom scores with that context rather than in isolation. The study does not show that changing sleep changes symptoms or recovery.
paper.athleteDev: This is not a performance study. The applied point is that sleep hours and concussion history should be recorded alongside baseline or post-injury testing data so that symptom and cognitive scores are read in context.
paper.rtp: The study supports considering sleep duration and concussion history when assessing post-concussion symptoms and planning management, as the authors conclude. It cannot show that longer sleep speeds recovery or that either factor should set return-to-play timing, because the design is retrospective and no return-to-play outcome is reported.

records.sourceFile: Effect of diagnosed sleep disorders on baseline concussion symptom cognitive and baseline assessments in collegiate athletes.pdf

paper.citation: McAllister-Deitrick J, Trbovich AM, Broglio SP, McCrea M, McAllister TW, Kontos AP. Effect of Diagnosed Sleep Disorders on Baseline Concussion Symptom, Cognitive, and Balance Assessments in Collegiate Athletes. Am J Sports Med. 2020;1-9.
paper.abstract: In 666 NCAA student-athletes (333 with a reported diagnosed sleep disorder, 333 matched controls), athletes with a sleep disorder reported higher affective and concussion symptoms at baseline and scored lower on the Standardized Assessment of Concussion, while they had fewer errors on the Balance Error Scoring System. There were no group differences on ImPACT. The authors conclude that clinicians should consider reported sleep disorders when interpreting baseline and post-injury concussion assessments, while noting that the differences are small.
paper.tldr: Among 666 collegiate athletes, those with a reported diagnosed sleep disorder had more baseline symptoms and emotional distress and scored slightly lower on a cognitive screen, but showed no ImPACT differences. The differences are small, so sleep disorder history should be noted when reading baseline and post-injury results.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study across 30 NCAA institutions in the CARE Consortium. Athletes with a self-reported diagnosed sleep disorder were matched by age, sex, sport and concussion history to controls without one. Baseline BESS, BSI-18, ImPACT, PCSS, SCAT5 and SAC were compared using one-way ANCOVAs adjusted for learning disability, ADHD and migraine history, with Bonferroni correction.
paper.findings: Athletes with a sleep disorder reported higher BSI-18 global severity (4.85 vs 2.30), PCSS (8.84 vs 4.04) and SCAT5 symptom severity (9.46 vs 4.48), with significant ANCOVA results (P < .01). They also had fewer BESS errors (12.93 vs 14.52; P = .003) and lower SAC scores (26.86 vs 27.30; P = .037), and the authors state the SAC difference is under one point. There were no group differences on ImPACT composites, and reported sleep the night before testing did not differ significantly (6.41 vs 6.72 hours; P = .087).
paper.limitations: The design is cross-sectional, so the associations cannot be read causally, and sleep disorder type, treatment and onset were not recorded. ImPACT data were available for 148 of 333 sleep-disorder athletes but 273 of 333 controls, so the null ImPACT result rests on unequal subsets. Effect sizes were small, the BESS result runs against the symptom findings and the authors call it anomalous, and the group differences in learning disability, ADHD and migraine history may influence the results.
paper.practicalImplications: When an athlete has a reported diagnosed sleep disorder, record it alongside baseline results and note that symptom scores such as the PCSS, SCAT5 and BSI-18 may be higher at baseline. Compare post-injury symptoms with that athlete's own baseline rather than with a norm alone. Take learning disability, ADHD and migraine history at the same time, since they were also more common in the sleep-disorder group.
paper.athleteDev: The paper concerns baseline testing rather than training or performance. It does not measure athletic performance, and its balance result (fewer BESS errors in athletes with diagnosed sleep disorders) was unexpected, so it should not be used to judge balance or training status.
paper.rtp: The study measures baseline performance only and does not track recovery or return-to-play decisions. The authors suggest baseline results and sleep disorder history may influence return-to-play and return-to-learning decisions, but the study cannot show how sleep disorders change return-to-play timing.

records.sourceFile: Effects of Repetitive Head Impacts on a Concussion Assessment Battery.pdf

paper.citation: Caccese JB, Best C, Lamond LC, DiFabio M, Kaminski TW, Watson D, et al. Effects of Repetitive Head Impacts on a Concussion Assessment Battery. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2019 (published ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Prospective study of 38 collegiate football and women's soccer players who completed a concussion assessment battery before and after one season, with head impacts recorded across the season. Few measures changed in a clinically meaningful way; the few significant associations were between high-magnitude impacts (above 98 g) and poorer visual memory, tandem gait and King-Devick performance.
paper.tldr: Across one collegiate season, repetitive head impacts were not linked to clinically meaningful change on a concussion battery. A few exploratory associations with high-magnitude impacts were found, and these need confirmation before anyone acts on them.
paper.methods: Pre-season and post-season testing of tandem gait, SAC, BESS, King-Devick, clinical reaction time and ImPACT composites in 15 male football and 23 women's soccer players, with impacts recorded by the HITS (football) or SIM (soccer) system. Direct-entry linear regressions tested impact exposure against change in each measure, with a group-by-time MANOVA; significance was set at P < 0.05 with no correction for multiple comparisons.
paper.findings: Among women's soccer players, more impacts above 98 g predicted worse Visual Memory (R2 = 0.670, P = 0.002) and Tandem Gait (R2 = 0.636, P = 0.029); among football players, more impacts above 98 g predicted worse King-Devick time (R2 = 0.756, P = 0.013). Overall time effect was significant (P = 0.006), and most measures improved from pre- to post-season in both groups, with Tandem Gait and King-Devick improving more in women's soccer than football (P = 0.001 and 0.048).
paper.limitations: There was no non-contact control group, and the two sports used different accelerometer systems, so impact magnitudes cannot be compared across sports. The authors ran 30 regression analyses without correction (Bonferroni would give P = 0.002), the football sample was 15 players, and impacts above 98 g were rare (mean 0.2, SD 0.4 per player in women's soccer and 1.1, SD 1.0 in football), so the significant associations rest on very few high-magnitude impacts. The authors state that the battery's learning effects may explain the post-season improvements.
paper.practicalImplications: This study does not support changing concussion screening on the basis of season-long impact counts, because the only significant links were exploratory and the battery showed no clinically meaningful change. Staff tracking head impacts may note that high-magnitude impacts, rather than total exposure, were the variable linked to the few worse scores, and test this in a larger cohort with a control group before acting on it.
paper.athleteDev: The paper gives no basis for changing training or performance programming. Season-long head impact exposure produced few significant associations with the concussion battery, and none that the authors call clinically meaningful.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-play decisions after a concussion. It tested athletes medically cleared for full participation who had no concussion in the prior 60 days, so the results do not apply to athletes after a diagnosed injury.

records.sourceFile: Effects of contact-collision sport history on gait in early to mid-adulthood.pdf

paper.citation: Hunzinger KJ, Caccese JB, Mannix R, Meehan WP, Hafer JF, Swanik CB, et al. Effects of contact/collision sport history on gait in early to mid-adulthood. Journal of Sport and Health Science. 2022 (article in press).
paper.abstract: Repetitive head impacts from contact and collision sports may affect later brain health, but evidence on gait in early and mid-adulthood is limited. This study compared single-task and dual-task gait in 113 adults across four groups, including former rugby players with prolonged head impact exposure. The authors report no significant group differences in gait after adjustment, and no prediction of gait from contact-sport career duration.
paper.tldr: In mostly young, physically active adults, past contact-sport participation, including prolonged rugby, was not linked to differences in walking speed, stride length or double support. Career duration did not predict gait, but the study was small and cross-sectional.
paper.methods: Participants were non-athletes who were not active, active non-contact athletes, active former high-risk contact-sport athletes, and active former rugby players with prolonged repetitive head impact exposure. Gait speed, stride length and double support were measured with three inertial sensors during single-task walking and walking with a cognitive task, and dual-task cost was calculated. Groups were compared with analysis of covariance adjusted for age, sex, concussion history and BMI, and career duration was tested with regression in the two contact-sport groups.
paper.findings: After adjustment, no group differences reached significance for any single-task, dual-task or dual-task cost gait variable (all P > 0.05). Adjusted single-task gait speed ranged from 1.04 m/s in former rugby players to 1.12 m/s in non-contact athletes. Career duration did not significantly predict gait in the contact-sport groups; one single-task double support model was significant overall (P = 0.009), but career duration did not add to it (P = 0.058).
paper.limitations: The sample was small (27 to 29 per group) and mostly under 50, with sex composition that differed considerably across groups (not statistically significant, adjusted for), career duration as a crude proxy for head impact exposure, and self-reported yes or no physical activity; survivor or volunteer bias is possible. The Table 3 footnote says there were significant group differences, which conflicts with the Results and abstract (all P > 0.05). The abstract conclusion generalizes to neurobehavioral function and the Conclusion refers to postural control, although only gait was measured, and the study did not include older or inactive former players.
paper.practicalImplications: For physically active adults in early to mid-adulthood, this study does not show that past contact-sport participation changes walking or dual-task gait. Staff should not use these null results to rule out later effects, especially in older or inactive former players.
paper.athleteDev: The study measured walking and dual-task gait, not sport performance, so it gives no basis for changing training loads or performance plans for current athletes. Its relevance is to neurobehavioral screening of former players.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It excluded participants with a concussion in the prior 6 months and did not test athletes returning after concussion or injury.

records.sourceFile: Elevated brain temperature under severe heat exposure impairs cortical motor activity and executive function.pdf

paper.citation: Tan XR, Stephenson MC, Alhadad SB, Loh KWZ, Soong TW, Lee JKW, et al. Elevated brain temperature under severe heat exposure impairs cortical motor activity and executive function. Journal of Sport and Health Science. 2023. Article in press.
paper.abstract: Eleven healthy males were studied with MRI at rest and after four conditions: exertional hyperthermia, passive hyperthermia, exertional hyperthermia with blended ice ingestion, and a seated control. Brain temperature was measured by MR spectroscopy, with cerebral perfusion, motor task activation and Stroop task activation also assessed.
paper.tldr: In healthy men, severe heat raised brain temperature and reduced motor cortex activity during a plantarflexion task, and passive heating reduced Stroop accuracy. Ice slurry ingestion lessened the rise in core and brain temperature, but the study is small and laboratory-based and did not measure sport performance.
paper.methods: Crossover design with 11 males (VO2peak 59 mL/kg/min). Each completed a familiarisation session and then four trials at least 7 days apart. Scans before and after each trial measured brain temperature by MR spectroscopy, cerebral blood flow by ASL, motor cortex BOLD during plantarflexion at 60% and 80% maximal voluntary contraction, and BOLD during a Stroop task.
paper.findings: Resting brain temperature was about 0.6 C higher than rectal temperature (37.3 vs 36.7 C) and rose to match rectal temperature after exertional heating, but stayed lower than rectal temperature after passive heating. Left precentral BOLD activity fell after exertional (P = .009) and passive (P = .006) heating but not after ice ingestion, and global grey matter perfusion fell after passive heating (P = .016). Stroop reaction times were faster after the exercise trials, while overall Stroop accuracy fell only after passive heating (P = .017).
paper.limitations: Rectal temperature could not be held above 38.5 C during scans, and sweat losses were under 3% of body mass. The sample was small (n=11), all were healthy young males not described as athletes, and the trials were single acute exposures in a laboratory.
paper.practicalImplications: Severe heat reduced motor cortex activity during a high-force plantarflexion task, and passive heating reduced Stroop accuracy. Ice slurry before and during exercise lowered rectal temperature and the left precentral activity drop was not seen in that trial. Whether these brain changes affect sport performance was not tested, and the sample was not athletes.
paper.athleteDev: The findings suggest pre-exercise and in-exercise cooling may protect neural function under heat stress, but sport performance was not measured. Cooling should be tested in sport settings before it is planned as a performance strategy.
paper.rtp: The study tested healthy volunteers, not injured players, and says nothing about return to sport after heat illness.

records.sourceFile: Estimated age of first exposure to contact sports is not associated with greater symptoms or worse cognitive functioning in male US service academy athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Caccese JB, Iverson GL, Cameron KL, Houston MN, McGinty GT, Jackson JC, et al. Estimated Age of First Exposure to Contact Sports Is Not Associated with Greater Symptoms or Worse Cognitive Functioning in Male U.S. Service Academy Athletes. Journal of Neurotrauma. 2020;37:334-339.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined whether estimated age of first exposure to contact sport was associated with pre-season ImPACT neurocognitive scores and symptom ratings in male service academy NCAA athletes. No association was found between early exposure, contact sport participation and cognitive or symptom outcomes. Learning accommodation history was linked to lower visual motor speed, and older age to faster reaction time and lower symptom severity.
paper.tldr: In male collegiate athletes at US service academies, starting a contact sport before age 12 was not linked to lower baseline cognitive scores or higher symptom ratings. This is a single-time-point study, so it does not show that early exposure is harmless over a lifetime.
paper.methods: Pre-season ImPACT baseline tests were collected from 891 male cadets, and 889 were analyzed for cognitive scores (826 for symptoms). Participants were split into contact (lacrosse, wrestling, ice hockey, soccer, rugby) and non-contact sports, and each group into estimated age of first exposure below or at least 12 years. Generalized linear models tested group, exposure, their interaction and covariates for learning accommodation, concussion history and age.
paper.findings: The group-by-exposure interaction was not significant for verbal memory (P = 0.788), visual memory (P = 0.100), visual motor speed (P = 0.780), reaction time (P = 0.955) or symptom severity (P = 0.090). Learning accommodation history was associated with lower visual motor speed (B = -2.97, P = 0.013). Older age was associated with faster reaction time (P = 0.036) and lower symptom severity (P = 0.019).
paper.limitations: Age of first exposure was estimated from self-reported years of participation and assumed continuous, the design is cross-sectional, and only men were studied. The authors note ImPACT and symptom reporting may be too insensitive to detect small differences and that pre-season under-reporting of symptoms is possible. The abstract and methods state N = 891, but the subgroup and sport counts sum to 889, which is the analyzed sample (826 for symptoms); one author reports research funding from ImPACT Applications.
paper.practicalImplications: This cross-sectional result does not support using an early contact-sport start age to flag collegiate male athletes for lower baseline cognitive scores or higher symptom ratings. Learning accommodation history (a small subgroup) was linked to lower visual motor speed, which supports recording it when interpreting baseline ImPACT scores.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not show that early contact-sport start age changes baseline cognition in these athletes, so start age should not be used alone to set cognitive expectations. It does not test whether exposure affects cognition or symptoms later in life.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The study used pre-season baseline testing only, and it did not assess athletes after a concussion or track recovery over time.

records.sourceFile: Evaluation of Executive Function and Mental Health in Retired Contact Sport Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Willer BS, Tiso M, Haider MN, Hinds AL, Baker JG, Miecznikowski JC, et al. Evaluation of Executive Function and Mental Health in Retired Contact Sport Athletes. J Head Trauma Rehabil. 2018:E1-E7.
paper.abstract: Comparison of 21 retired professional NFL and NHL players with 21 age-matched noncontact sport athletes on self-report, informant report, neuropsychological tests, and mood and personality measures.
paper.tldr: Retired professional contact sport athletes reported some executive function problems, but objective tests and spouse reports showed no differences from controls. They did have more anxiety, which deserves follow-up.
paper.methods: Case-control design. Executive function was measured with the BRIEF-A (self and spouse report), the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, D-KEFS, Trail Making, digit span, list learning, verbal fluency and digit symbol. Mood and personality were measured with the BDI, BAI and PID-5. Group comparisons used unequal-variance t tests with Cohen's d.
paper.findings: Players rated themselves more impaired on working memory and initiation subscales than controls, but spouse reports and objective executive tests showed no significant differences. Raw depression scores were higher in players (BDI 10.2 vs 3.8, P=.004), though within the normal range, and 7 of 21 players versus 0 of 21 controls met the anxiety threshold. Psychoticism was higher in players, driven by the unusual beliefs and experiences facet, and remained within norms.
paper.limitations: Small sample of 21 per group, with volunteers who said worry about their mental health was a main reason for joining. No formal effort testing was done. The controls were endurance-trained noncontact athletes whom the authors describe as a superior aging population, and they scored below norms on psychoticism, which inflates some group differences.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians seeing retired contact sport athletes should screen for anxiety, which was more common in this group, rather than assume broad executive decline. Self-reported working memory or task initiation problems should be checked with objective testing and informant reports.
paper.athleteDev: Retired contact sport athletes in this study reported some working memory and task-initiation problems, but objective tests showed no differences from controls. Anxiety screening may matter more than assuming executive decline.
paper.rtp: The study concerns retired players, not athletes recovering from injury, so it cannot guide return-to-sport or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Examination of reaction time deficits following concussion - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Lempke LB, Howell DR, Eckner JT, Lynall RC. Examination of Reaction Time Deficits Following Concussion: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2020.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 60 studies (9,688 participants) on reaction time after concussion. Acute deficits were medium-to-large in both between-subject and within-subject designs, persisted to 21 to 59 days in the between-subject analysis, and were not significant at 80 to 365 days.
paper.tldr: Reaction time is slower after concussion in the first 3 days, with medium-to-large effects in both study designs. Between-subject deficits lingered to about 59 days, beyond typical clinical recovery, but the clinical meaning of those lingering deficits is not yet established.
paper.methods: PRISMA-guided searches of PubMed, CINAHL and EBSCOhost (January 2002 to March 2019) were screened independently by two reviewers. Hedges' d effects were calculated separately for between-subject (concussed vs control) and within-subject (post-injury vs baseline) designs. Mixed-effects multilevel models with restricted maximum likelihood accounted for nested effects, and moderators were examined in acute effects, with time since injury binned into acute, sub-acute, intermediate and long-term periods.
paper.findings: Acute deficits were D+ = -0.73 (95% CI -0.99 to -0.46) between-subject and -0.75 (95% CI -0.91 to -0.59) within-subject. Between-subject deficits remained at 4 to 17 days (D+ = -0.57) and 21 to 59 days (D+ = -0.32, p = 0.025), with no significant deficit at 80 to 365 days (D+ = 0.35, 95% CI -0.48 to 1.18). Sex (% male) was the only significant between-subject moderator (about -0.017 per 1% male), while RT measure type (simple vs mixed) and computerized platform (ANAM, HeadMinder CRI, ImPACT) differed within-subject; all category estimates were negative, although the ANAM within-subject interval crossed zero (-0.37, 95% CI -0.77 to 0.03).
paper.limitations: Pooled effects were highly heterogeneous, funnel and Q-Q plots showed asymmetry (Egger's test significant), and 22 studies were excluded for lacking numerical data. The within-subject analysis could not examine intermediate or long-term timeframes, and the intermediate-term between-subject result rests on 26 effects. Study quality was moderate (mean Newcastle-Ottawa scores 7.41 and 7.56), and most studies used high school or college athletes or military personnel.
paper.practicalImplications: Reaction time should be one part of a multi-part concussion assessment, since it is slower in the first 3 days after injury and the authors say the method matters less than using reliable, valid tools. The authors state that these findings are not a reason to drop pre-injury baselines, because reaction time is only one component of the battery. Staff should avoid judging concussed athletes only against orthopaedic-injured controls, which the authors suggest may not be the best comparison.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not address training or performance enhancement. Its relevance to performance is the authors' view that reaction time likely has not fully recovered when athletes return to sport, so staff should not assume reaction time has normalised at clearance.
paper.rtp: The review directly addresses recovery timing, reporting that reaction-time deficits extend beyond typical clinical recovery and that reaction time likely has not truly recovered at return to sport. It cannot show when return is safe, because the clinical consequences of lingering deficits are unknown and return-to-play decisions were not studied.

records.sourceFile: Examining whether loss of consciousness is associated with worse performance on the SCAT5 and slower clinical recovery after concussion in professional athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Iverson GL, Gaudet CE, Kissinger-Knox A, Gardner AJ. Examining Whether Loss of Consciousness Is Associated With Worse Performance on the SCAT5 and Slower Clinical Recovery After Concussion in Professional Athletes. Journal of Neurotrauma. 2023;40:2330-2340.
paper.abstract: Video review of head impact events in three National Rugby League seasons identified possible loss of consciousness (LOC) in 99 of 1,706 events (5.8%). In diagnosed concussions, possible LOC was linked to worse Maddocks question scores but not to games missed or time to medical clearance.
paper.tldr: Brief possible loss of consciousness seen on video may be more common than self-report studies suggest, and in diagnosed concussions it was linked to more Maddocks orientation and memory errors. It did not predict games missed or days to medical clearance in this professional league.
paper.methods: Analysis of head impact events from 201 matches per season in the National Rugby League (2017 to 2019), with possible LOC defined from physician removal for suspected LOC plus video signs, or both video signs (no protective action in the fall, unresponsiveness or lying motionless), and duration timed on video by one senior author. Players removed for a Head Injury Assessment completed the SCAT5, including Maddocks questions, the Standardized Assessment of Concussion (SAC) and modified Balance Error Scoring System (mBESS). Groups were compared with chi-square and Mann-Whitney U tests, with odds ratios and Cohen's d as effect sizes and Benjamini-Hochberg correction (alpha 0.01).
paper.findings: In the 255 medically diagnosed concussions, players with possible LOC scored lower on the Maddocks questions (mean 4.0 vs 4.6 of 5, p < 0.01), but did not differ on SAC total score, orientation, memory, concentration, mBESS errors or symptom endorsement. Possible LOC was not associated with missed games (21.5% vs 14.0% missed one or more games, p = 0.164) or days to medical clearance (7.8 vs 7.4 days, p = 0.486). In the full sample of 661 athletes with SCAT5 data, possible LOC was linked to more symptoms and lower SAC and Maddocks scores.
paper.limitations: Possible LOC was judged from video rather than observed by a clinician, and duration was timed by stopwatch with uncertain reliability. The authors note possible circularity, because seeing LOC may raise the expectation of concussion and the SCAT5 is part of the diagnosis, and a single rater coded all videos. In the full sample the abstract lists worse concentration, but Table 2 gives p = 0.03 against the study alpha of 0.01; only 20 possible-LOC cases without a diagnosed concussion had SCAT5 data.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors conclude that concussion should be managed on clinical evaluation and individual needs rather than differently because of LOC, since possible LOC did not predict games missed or days to clearance. Possible LOC was linked to more Maddocks errors on the sideline, although the authors note Maddocks questions have not shown high sensitivity for concussion in prior rugby research. Video signs indicate only possible LOC, because the authors state LOC can usually only be determined definitively by a provider who observes it.
paper.athleteDev: The study concerns concussion assessment rather than training or performance, and it reports no performance outcome. Staff should not use it to judge an athlete's on-field performance after a head impact.
paper.rtp: The study directly addresses return to play: in medically diagnosed concussions, possible LOC was not associated with games missed or days to medical clearance. Because it covers one professional league and relies on video identification, staff should not use this finding alone to shorten or lengthen a return-to-play timeline.

records.sourceFile: Exercising more than 150 min per week after concussion is associated with sleep quality improvements.pdf

paper.citation: Howell DR, Wingerson MJ, Smulligan KL, Magliato S, Simon S, Wilson JC. Exercising More Than 150 min/wk After Concussion Is Associated With Sleep Quality Improvements. J Head Trauma Rehabil. 2023.
paper.abstract: Prospective observational cohort of adolescents with concussion, who wore a wrist-worn activity tracker between clinic visits about 1 and 5 weeks after injury. Participants who averaged more than 150 min/wk of aerobic exercise showed greater improvement in Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores than those who exercised 150 min/wk or less, and weekly exercise volume predicted sleep improvement after adjustment for age and migraine history.
paper.tldr: Adolescents with concussion who averaged more than 150 minutes per week of aerobic exercise between visits showed greater sleep quality improvement than those who exercised less. The study is observational, so it cannot show that the exercise caused the improvement.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort of adolescents aged 10 to 17 years with concussion, first assessed within 18 days of injury (mean 8 days) and again about 5 weeks later. Sleep was measured with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and symptoms with the Post-Concussion Symptom Inventory. Exercise was recorded with a wrist-worn activity tracker and grouped at 150 min/wk, and a multivariable regression used weekly exercise volume as a continuous predictor, adjusted for age and migraine history.
paper.findings: Fifteen participants (42%) exercised more than 150 min/wk and 21 exercised 150 min/wk or less. The higher-volume group had greater improvement in PSQI scores (median change 5 [IQR 3, 7] vs 1 [0, 4]; P = .008; Cohen d 0.96), and PSQI scores did not differ significantly between groups at the first visit. Each additional hour of weekly exercise was associated with an expected 0.82-point greater PSQI improvement (95% CI 0.26 to 1.38; P = .005).
paper.limitations: The observational design means causality and direction cannot be determined, because better sleep may also allow more exercise, although the abstract conclusion uses causal wording ('led to'). Sleep was self-reported and not measured objectively, and 7 of 43 enrolled adolescents were excluded for loss to follow-up or not wearing the tracker. The two groups differed in age, sex and migraine history at a trend level (P = .06 to .09), and preexisting conditions were self-reported.
paper.practicalImplications: Counsel adolescents with concussion on both exercise and sleep habits, since higher weekly exercise was associated with better sleep recovery in this cohort. The study points to a volume above 150 min/wk, but it did not test exercise as a treatment, so the figure should be presented as an association and not as a prescription. Track sleep quality alongside symptoms during the subacute phase, since sleep quality changed differently between exercise groups in this cohort and the study measured it separately from symptom severity.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not measure performance and does not show that more than 150 min/wk of aerobic exercise is appropriate for athletic training after concussion. It is only relevant to the return of training volume in that it links higher weekly exercise with better sleep quality in this group.
paper.rtp: Limited direct relevance, since the study does not address return-to-play decisions. Time to symptom resolution did not differ significantly between the groups (23 vs 29 days; P = .31), but sleep quality may be an additional recovery domain to monitor during the subacute phase.
